newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Communist chief raps Yeltsin's Helsinki diplomacy.
newsitem.headline: Communist chief raps Yeltsin's Helsinki diplomacy.

text.p: Russian Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov blasted Boris Yeltsin's foreign policy on Friday, saying the president was incapable of defending Moscow's interests at his summit talks with U.S. President Bill Clinton.
"Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin) has not had any victories for a long time, except over his own people and country," Zyuganov told reporters in the State Duma lower house of parliament.
"I don't believe in his international successes. Everything he does is linked to destruction," said Zyuganov.
He was speaking as Yeltsin and Clinton met in Helsinki to discuss NATO expansion and arms control. U.S. aides described the talks as "substantive and intense".

Opposition to NATO's plans to admit former communist countries in eastern and central Europe is one of the few issues that Yeltsin and his communist and ultra-nationalist foes in the Duma are able to agree on.
Russia regards the plans as a threat to its own security that will create new division lines in post-Cold War Europe.
"NATO expansion is a mistake," Zyuganov said, adding that Moscow had the industrial might to thwart it. He did not elaborate.

Yeltsin, whose aides have kept up a furious verbal offensive against NATO's plans ahead of Friday's summit talks, also came under fire from Vladimir Zhirinovsky's ultra-nationalist Liberal Democratic Party (LDPR), one of the biggest Duma parties.

"So long as we possess nuclear rockets and forces of nuclear deterrence...dialogue with our opponents can proceed very concretely, as it would have done 10 years ago," Interfax news agency quoted senior LDPR deputy Alexei Mitrofanov as saying.
The communists have prepared a draft resolution calling on Yeltsin and the government to rule out Russia itself joining the Western alliance.

Neither NATO nor Moscow have suggested this as a serious possibility, but the resolution, which might be debated later on Friday, is seen as a symbolic gesture to put added pressure on Yeltsin during his talks with Clinton.
